opus-5.5.text:
I think the place it matters most is the developing world. There's a natural tendency for a technology like this to flow first to the places that are already rich: the companies with the biggest budgets, the countries with the best infrastructure, the people who are already plugged into the global economy. If we just let things take their course, I worry we end up in a world where AI cures a bunch of diseases and drives incredible economic growth in, say, the US and Western Europe, while sub-Saharan Africa or parts of South Asia get it ten or twenty years later, if at all. That would be a real moral failure, because those are the places where the marginal benefit is the largest.

Health is probably the clearest example. A lot of the biggest killers in poorer countries, like malaria, tuberculosis, and neglected tropical diseases, are problems where AI-accelerated biology could plausibly make enormous progress. But discovering a cure isn't the same as delivering it. You need distribution, manufacturing, health systems, and trust from local populations. Historically that's been the bottleneck, not the science. So even if the science gets dramatically faster, you need deliberate effort on the deployment side: working with governments, with organizations that already know how to get vaccines and treatments into rural areas, and making sure pricing and IP arrangements don't lock people out.

The second area is economic growth more broadly. I'm genuinely hopeful that AI could help developing economies grow much faster, in the way that some East Asian economies caught up in the twentieth century. But that won't happen automatically. It requires those countries to have the compute, the connectivity, and the human capital to actually use these systems, and it requires the systems to work well in their languages and their contexts. That's something companies like ours, and governments, have to actively invest in rather than assume it'll trickle down.

And then there's a subtler one within rich countries too: making sure the gains don't just accrue to a small number of people who own the capital or the models. If AI starts doing a large fraction of cognitive work, we need to think seriously about how the benefits get shared, whether through policy, taxation, or new institutions. I don't think anyone has fully figured that out yet, but I'd rather we start thinking about it now than wait until the disruption is already here.

So to summarize: the developing world first and foremost, especially health and economic development, and then distributional questions within societies. In all of these the default trajectory isn't good enough. It has to be deliberate.

r001.rationale: The response cites wealth, infrastructure, and deployment barriers, but does not identify poorly functioning markets as a reason the developing world may be left behind.

r002.rationale: It does not mention rural Americans or compare their access to cures with the developing world’s access problem.

r003.rationale: It says health benefits require deliberate deployment efforts and that progress will not happen automatically.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, and the way I'd frame it is that the benefits of AI are not going to distribute themselves evenly by default. The market will do a lot, and I don't want to understate that. If you have a model that can cure diseases or design better crops or tutor every kid in the world, a lot of that gets out just through normal commercial channels because people want it. But there are some pretty clear places where the default dynamics don't get you there, and those are where I think you need deliberate effort.

The first one is health, and particularly health in the developing world. If you look at the history of something like malaria or tuberculosis, the science has often been there for decades before the delivery happened. The bottleneck wasn't knowledge, it was distribution, cost, infrastructure, political will. My worry is that AI could compress the scientific timeline enormously, we could get to a place where we know how to prevent or treat a huge range of diseases, and then the actual lives saved lag by twenty or thirty years because nobody prioritized getting it to the places that need it most. That's the kind of gap where you need governments, philanthropy, international institutions, and honestly the AI companies themselves to lean in. I've said before I think the labs have some obligation here, and I mean that.

The second is economic. There's a real risk that the gains from AI concentrate in a small number of companies and a small number of countries, and that the people whose jobs get disrupted see very little of the upside. I don't think the answer is to slow the technology down, because the benefits are too large. But I do think we need to be deliberate about things like how the wealth gets shared, what the tax structure looks like, what the social safety net looks like in a world where a lot of cognitive labor is automated. Those aren't problems the technology solves on its own. They're political and institutional problems, and they're the kind of thing that tends to get addressed late, after a lot of damage has been done, unless people start working on them early.

And then the third, which is maybe less obvious, is just access to the models themselves. If the frontier is held by a handful of actors, then who gets to use it, on what terms, in which languages, for which problems, becomes a really consequential set of decisions. I think there's a version of this where a researcher in Nairobi or Dhaka has the same tools as someone in San Francisco, and a version where they don't, and the difference between those two worlds over a few decades is enormous. Some of that is pricing, some of it is infrastructure like compute and connectivity, some of it is just whether the companies care enough to make it happen.

So if I had to summarize, I'd say the places where deliberate effort matters most are the ones where the people who benefit most are the ones with the least ability to pay or to demand it. Global health, the displaced worker, the researcher without resources. The technology can get us ninety percent of the way on the science, and then the last ten percent, which is actually where the lives are, requires people to decide it matters.

r001.rationale: The response says commercial markets will not ensure delivery in some cases and describes developing-world health benefits being delayed by distribution, cost, infrastructure, and lack of prioritization.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the developing-world access problem with rural Americans lacking access to cures.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says delivering health benefits to the developing world requires governments, philanthropy, institutions, and AI companies to make a deliberate effort.

astra-6.text:
I think the place where deliberate effort is most needed is making sure that people who have the least economic power can still benefit. If AI helps us develop much better treatments for disease, that’s enormously valuable. But developing a treatment and getting it to someone in a poor country are two different problems. You still need distribution, you need a functioning health system, and someone has to pay for it.

So I’d look particularly at global health and education. Can someone in a rural area get high-quality medical advice? Can a child whose school has very few resources get access to a really good tutor? Those are places where the potential benefit is huge, but the market incentive to serve those people may be relatively weak.

And I’d distinguish access to the technology from access to the wealth it creates. You could make an AI system very cheap and still end up with the economic gains concentrated among a small number of people. Making sure those gains translate into broadly better lives is a separate problem, and I don’t think technology companies can solve it on their own.

r001.rationale: It says market incentives to serve people in poor countries may be weak, identifying a market-related reason they could miss AI’s benefits.

r002.rationale: It mentions rural access to medical advice but does not compare rural Americans’ access to cures with the developing world’s access problem.

r003.rationale: It says deliberate effort is needed and explains that distributing treatments requires health systems and payment, rather than happening automatically.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the place where deliberate effort is most needed is making sure that people who don’t have economic or political power actually share in the benefits. There’s a difference between developing a technology that can do something extraordinary and getting that capability to the people who need it.

Take health. If AI helps us develop treatments for diseases, that’s an enormous achievement. But whether those treatments reach people in poor countries depends on things like cost, distribution, and the capacity of local health systems. Those problems don’t disappear just because the science gets better.

And then there’s the question of economic opportunity. Making a powerful model inexpensive and widely available could give a lot of people access to expertise they couldn’t otherwise afford. That would be very valuable. But access to a model isn’t the same thing as sharing in the wealth it creates, particularly if it also disrupts people’s jobs.

So I’d distinguish between making the capabilities broadly accessible and making sure the economic gains are broadly shared. I’m optimistic about what the technology can enable, but I don’t think either of those outcomes is something we should simply assume will happen.

r001.rationale: The response cites cost, distribution, and local health-system capacity as barriers, but does not identify poorly functioning markets as a reason the developing world may be left behind.

r002.rationale: It discusses access to treatments in poor countries but does not compare that problem with rural Americans potentially lacking access to cures.

r003.rationale: It says treatment access depends on practical factors that science alone does not fix, and that broad sharing should not be assumed—communicating the need for deliberate effort.
